Reviewer #2 :
Gu et al. present a well-executed study that combines single-cell and spatial
transcriptomic analyses to dissect the immune-tumor interactions underlying
therapeutic resistance in advanced aRCC. The integration of multi-omics data with
clinical response information and experimental validation is impressive, and the work
provides mechanistic insights with relatively clear translational relevance. The
identification of the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 axis as a driver of immunosuppressive
TME and therapy resistance may open new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the encouraging comments and recognition of
our multi-omics integration and mechanistic findings. We appreciate the positive
assessment of the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis and its translational relevance. We
have revised the manuscript to further clarify key methodological details and improve
the presentation. We also added new in-vitro data supporting the direct effect of
SAA-stimulated neutrophils on CEACAM1 upregulation, which strengthens the
proposed mechanism. We are grateful for the reviewer’s constructive feedback.
Major Comments:
1. The manuscript identifies the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 axis as a potential
mechanistic pathway contributing to resistance to TKI plus ICI therapy. However,
much of this mechanistic link remains inferred from transcriptomic correlations and
ligand-receptor analyses. Although the authors demonstrate that SAA inhibition
enhances therapeutic efficacy in a mouse model, direct functional validation of the
key molecular players (e.g., SAA1/2, CEACAM1, and TIM-3) would greatly
strengthen the mechanistic claims, even just in cell-based systems. For example,
knockdown or overexpression studies in RCC cell lines, neutrophil co-culture assays,
or cytokine signaling blockade experiments could directly test the causality of these
interactions. At minimum, perturbation experiments in vitro would reinforce the
conclusion that this axis is mechanistically responsible for the observed phenotypes
rather than merely correlative.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In the revised
manuscript, we added a direct in vitro functional perturbation experiment
demonstrating that SAA stimulation upregulates CEACAM1 expression in neutrophils
(Response Fig. 2), providing functional evidence for the proposed SAA–CEACAM1
axis. In these experiments, neutrophils were freshly isolated from peripheral blood of
treatment-naïve RCC patients using CD15 magnetic bead–based separation (>99%
purity) and subsequently stimulated with recombinant human SAA protein.
To extend these findings in vivo, SAA inhibition reduced neutrophil infiltration
and enhanced the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in an RCC mouse model (Fig. 4d, g).
Importantly, mIHC analysis of clinical samples further validated these observations,
revealing a significantly higher proportion of CEACAM1+ neutrophils in
non-responders compared with responders (Fig. 2j), supporting the clinical relevance
of CEACAM1 upregulation in therapeutic resistance.
Moreover, the CEACAM1–TIM-3 interaction has been well established in prior
studies³⁻⁴, providing additional mechanistic support. Collectively, these
complementary in vitro, in vivo, and patient-derived data strengthen the causal link
between the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis and the establishment of an
immunosuppressive TME, ultimately driving resistance to TKI plus ICI therapy.
Regarding the reviewer’s suggestion for genetic perturbation experiments, we
note that the short lifespan and limited transfectability of primary neutrophils make
direct SAA knockdown technically challenging. Therefore, we employed recombinant
SAA protein to model its biological effects, an approach that is physiologically
relevant given that SAA functions as a secreted acute-phase protein.
Response Fig. 2 SAA stimulation upregulates CEACAM1 expression in RCC
patients’ neutrophils. (a) Representative flow cytometry histograms showing surface
CD66a/c/e expression in human neutrophils following stimulation with increasing
concentrations of recombinant human SAA (0, 250, 500, and 1,000 ng/mL) for 12
hours (now Fig. 4a in the revised manuscript). (b) Quantification of relative
CEACAM1 expression levels assessed by flow cytometry (left) and qRT-PCR (right)
under the indicated SAA concentrations. Each dot represents an independent sample
(n = 8). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. P values were calculated using an
unpaired two-sided t-test (now Fig. 4b in the revised manuscript). (c) Flow
cytometric gating strategy demonstrates efficient enrichment of CD15⁺ neutrophils
(>99% purity) following magnetic separation. Sequential gating excluded debris and
doublets prior to assessment of CD15 and CD66a/c/e expression (now
Supplementary Fig. 6b in the revised manuscript).
2. The manuscript reports several mechanistic findings involving SAA+ tumor cells,
VEGFA+ neutrophils, Tregs, CEACAM1-TIM-3 signaling, and angiogenesis. While
each of these findings is biologically meaningful, presenting them all in equal detail
makes the narrative somewhat diffuse. The authors may consider prioritizing one
central mechanism, such as the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 immunoregulatory loop, as
the main storyline, while condensing or relocating secondary mechanisms (e.g., Treg
involvement, VEGFA signaling). This refinement would sharpen the mechanistic
focus and help readers appreciate the central conceptual advance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion, which has
significantly helped refine the clarity of our mechanistic narrative. In the revised
manuscript, we have restructured the narrative to center on the SAA–CEACAM1–
TIM-3 immunoregulatory loop as the primary mechanistic axis driving
immunotherapy resistance in aRCC. To sharpen the mechanistic focus, content
describing secondary mechanisms including Treg infiltration, VEGFA+ neutrophil
mediated angiogenesis has been streamlined and concisely integrated into the main
Results section (Line 242-251, 300-302) . Through this revision, we aim to provide a
more focused and coherent narrative that enables readers to readily grasp the central
mechanistic insight of our study.
3. The spatial transcriptomic analyses provide valuable contextual information, but
the spatial localization of the SAA+ tumor regions relative to VEGFA+ neutrophils
and CD8+ T cells could be presented more quantitatively. Strengthening the link
between spatial proximity and inferred signaling axes, for instance, through
co-localization metrics or neighborhood enrichment analyses, would provide stronger
evidence for spatially coordinated immunoregulation. This integration would also
guide selection of targetable microenvironmental niches for future therapeutic
exploration.
Response: We thank the reviewer for giving us suggestions on how to improve our
work. We agree that a more quantitative spatial analysis would strengthen the link
between tumor-derived SAA and its immunomodulatory effects on VEGFA+
neutrophils and CD8+ T cells. We have carefully addressed this concern
through supplementary quantitative spatial analyzes, and the detailed revisions are
summarized below:
1. Spatial localization characteristics between SAA+ tumor regions
and VEGFA+ neutrophils
To clarify the spatial relationship between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils,
we stratified the TME into two distinct compartments including tumor core and tumor
margin. We observed distinct spatial distributions of SAA+ tumor cells between
responders and non-responders based on the deconvolution results generated by the
spotiphy algorithm. Notably, in non-responders, SAA+ tumor cells were predominantly
localized within the tumor core, with only a minor subset scattered in the tumor
margin (Response Fig. 3a). In contrast, VEGFA+ neutrophils are significantly enriched
in the tumor margin (Response Fig. 3b), a spatial domain that overlaps with the
distribution of these scattered SAA⁺ tumor cells (Response Fig. 3b).
Given that SAA is a secreted protein, we hypothesize that SAA produced by
tumor cells within the tumor core diffuses to the tumor margin and exerts paracrine
effects on VEGFA+ neutrophils. Supporting this model, the mIHC showed that both
VEGFA+ neutrophils (Fig. 2d) and SAA+ tumor cells (Fig. 3h) are significantly more
abundant in non-responders compared to responders after treatment, suggesting a
potential SAA–neutrophil axis in non-responders. Critically, our in vitro experiments
demonstrated that recombinant SAA significantly upregulates CEACAM1 expression
in RCC patients’s neutrophils (Response Fig. 2), indicating that tumor-derived SAA
can modulate neutrophil function independently of direct cell–cell contact.
Unexpectedly, the presence of scattered SAA+ tumor cells in the tumor margin
prompted us to further explore their potential interaction with VEGFA+ neutrophils,
particularly in non-responder patients. To test this hypothesis, we computed a
co-localization index between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils specifically
within the tumor margin, following a previously described analytical pipeline3.
Notably, our data demonstrated that non-responders (STpost3 and STpost4) exhibit
significantly higher co-localization indices compared to responders (STpost1 and
STpost2). This finding supports the potential interaction between SAA⁺ malignant
cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils in the tumor margin of non-responders. Comparative
analysis further revealed that patient STpost4 exhibited the highest co-localization
index among all patients (Response Fig. 3c). Importantly, clinical follow-up data
showed that STpost4 subsequently experienced tumor recurrence, suggesting that this
spatial co-localization may not only be associated with resistance to ICI plus TKI
combination therapy but also with disease progression (Supplementary Table 1).
Response Fig. 3 Spatial distribution of SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils.
(a-b) Boxplots showing the proportion of SAA+ tumor cells (a) and VEGFA+
neutrophils (b) across distinct tissue regions (tumor core vs. tumor margin) in four
patients. (c) Boxplots comparing the co-localization index between SAA+ tumor cells
and VEGFA+ neutrophils in the tumor margin across four patients. P values were
calculated using unpaired two-sided t-test. In all boxplots, the center line in the
boxplots indicates the median, the lower and upper hinges correspond to the first and
third quartiles, and the whiskers extend at most 1.5 times the interquartile range past
the upper and lower quartiles (Now Supplementary Fig. 5g-i in the revised
manuscript).
2. Quantitative analysis of spatial distance between CD8+ T cells
and VEGFA+ neutrophils
To further strengthen the characterization of the spatial regulatory network in TME,
we performed quantitative cell-cell distance measurement analysis focusing on
CD8+ T cells subsets and VEGFA+ neutrophils. To quantitatively assess the spatial
relationships between these cell subsets, we applied Kullback-Leibler (KL)
divergence analysis4,5. Density plots consistently revealed that VEGFA+ neutrophils
exhibited greater spatial similarity and pronounced co-localization with three CD8+ T
cells subsets (PD-1-TIM-3+, PD-1+TIM-3+, PD-1-TIM-3-), which was reflected by
lower KL divergence values (Response Fig. 4a-d). Notably, among all non-responder
patients (STpost3 and STpost4), the KL divergence values between VEGFA+
neutrophils and the three aforementioned CD8+ T cell subsets were below 2
(Response Fig. 4a-b). In contrast, higher KL divergence values were observed
between these cell populations in another responder sample (STpost2) (Response Fig.
4c). For STpost1, due to the extremely low proportion of VEGFA+ neutrophils
(Response Fig. 3b) obtained via deconvolution, co-localization analysis between
VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cells was not performed for this sample. We have
provided more details in the Methods session “Cell type co-localization analysis” in
the revised manuscript.
Response Fig. 4 Spatial co-localization between VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cell
subsets. (a-c) Spatial mapping of cell types onto spatial transcriptomics (ST) slides
from three post-treatment samples STpost3 (a), STpost4 (b), and STpost2 (c) using
the spotiphy deconvolution method. Color intensity represents estimated relative
abundance for all cell types (top left) and individual cell type (top right). The density
plots display the KL divergence of the observed co-localization pattern relative to a
null distribution derived from spatial permutation (bottom). (d) Boxplots comparing
the co-localization index between VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cell subsets
indicated in the tumor margin across three patients. P values were calculated using
two-sided Student’s t-test. In all boxplots, the center line in the boxplots indicates the
median, the lower and upper hinges correspond to the first and third quartiles, and the
whiskers extend at most 1.5 times the interquartile range past the upper and lower
quartiles (Now Fig.5e, Supplementary Fig. 10a, b in the revised manuscript)..
4. To further enhance the translational potential of the study, it would be beneficial to
discuss strategies for dual targeting of SAA and CEACAM1, given their
compensatory relationship. A clear statement on how these preclinical findings may
inform patient stratification or biomarker development in RCC would also strengthen
clinical relevance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the translational potential of
targeting SAA and CEACAM1, a point also raised by Reviewer #1. In response, we
have expanded the Discussion (Line 403-450) to explicitly address the translational
implications of these findings, including therapeutic strategies, patient stratification,
and biomarker development.
As now discussed, although SAA and CEACAM1 exhibit a compensatory
relationship, their druggability differs substantially. SAA, as a secreted acute-phase
protein, is less tractable as a direct therapeutic target, whereas CEACAM1 is a
membrane-bound receptor with higher target specificity. Consequently, simultaneous
dual targeting may be challenging in practice. Nevertheless, SAA remains a promising
predictive biomarker for immunotherapy response (Fig. 3j) and multiple independent
studies, including recent evidence in hepatocellular carcinoma6,7. We also
acknowledge that the current sample size for SAA-based analyzes is limited, and that
validation in larger, independent cohorts will be required to firmly establish its
predictive value and clinical applicability.
From a therapeutic perspective, our findings suggest a potential stratified
approach: SAA may serve as a biomarker to identify patients at risk of primary
resistance, while CEACAM1 represents a more actionable target for patients with
immune-refractory disease. In this context, re-challenge strategies targeting
CEACAM1 are conceptually supported by existing phase II clinical data on CM248.
Although CEACAM1-directed antibodies are not yet clinically available in China, we
are currently pursuing translational development through collaboration with a
domestic pharmaceutical partner (Junshi Biosciences Co., Ltd.) to advance
CEACAM1-targeted therapeutic strategies. Additional preclinical validation studies
are ongoing, and detailed data cannot be disclosed at this stage due to confidentiality
considerations.
Reviewer #3:
This study was conducted using clinical trial specimens together with public datasets
and focuses on the core challenge of resistance to combined immune-targeted therapy
in renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Through single-cell sequencing and humanized mouse
models, the authors propose a novel mechanism whereby tumor cell–neutrophil
interactions can mediate the resistance of immunotherapy combined with targeted
therapy in RCC.
Fit with Nature Communications: Nature Communications values mechanistic
discoveries that bridge fundamental biological understanding with clinical translation.
This study exemplifies that mission by beginning with clinically validated phenomena,
applying state-of-the-art single-cell technologies to interrogate the biological “black
box,” and completing the translational exploration preliminarily through further
validation in humanized mouse models. The conceptual design—spanning from
clinical observation to mechanistic exploration and translational
confirmation—closely aligns with the journal’s aim to publish conceptually
innovative and broadly relevant biomedical research.
Novel Mechanistic Point: The study reveals that VEGFA⁺ neutrophils (Neu_06) are
enriched in non-responders and specifically interact with SAA⁺ tumor cells. This
interaction promotes T-cell exhaustion through the CEACAM1–TIM3 ligand–
receptor axis, thereby establishing a new mechanistic framework linking metabolic
reprogramming in myeloid cells to adaptive immune dysfunction. Such a finding
provides an original and well-supported explanation for resistance to immunotherapy
combined with targeted therapy in RCC.
Translational Value: Using RCC samples from patients with distinct efficacy and
some public datasets, the study identifies actionable pathways driving resistance. The
demonstration that inhibition of SAA in Balb/c mice or pharmacologic blockade of
CEACAM1–TIM3 signaling in humanized mouse models can both enhance treatment
efficacy, which confers strong translational value. These results not only support
biomarker-based patient stratification but also propose combination therapeutic
strategies with the potential to improve outcomes in patients who are super-resistant
to current immunotherapies—a population with critical unmet clinical needs.
I recommend Minor Revision for this manuscript. The study is robust overall, but a
few targeted refinements are needed to maximize its clarity and impact prior to
acceptance. The required revisions are primarily clarifications and minor additional
analyses; no fundamental flaws are present. Addressing the points below will ensure
the manuscript achieves its full potential for a high-impact venue.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thorough and encouraging assessment of our
study and for recommending Minor Revisions. We appreciate the recognition of our
integrated approach combining clinical samples, public datasets, single-cell analyzes,
and humanized mouse models to uncover the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3–mediated
mechanism of immunotherapy resistance in RCC. In response, we have clarified
methodological details, emphasized the central mechanistic storyline, slightly
extended the mechanistic discussion, and polished the presentation. We believe these
revisions further strengthen the clarity, rigor, and overall impact of the manuscript for
the Nature Communications readership.
Major Concerns:
1. Role and differentiation trajectory of neutrophils
Neutrophils are a critical component of the tumor microenvironment. In Figure 1c, the
predictive index indicates that baseline neutrophil abundance shows the strongest
negative correlation with response to ICI+TKI in RCC, thereby justifying the authors’
focus on neutrophil subclusters. The study further suggests that differentiation from
Neu_01 to Neu_02 mediates therapeutic response, while differentiation from Neu_01
to Neu_06 contributes to resistance. In Figure 2e, Neu_01 shows the most negative
correlation with efficacy in the predictive index, yet its dynamic change in the
treatment index is most positively correlated with therapeutic response. Given that
Neu_01 can differentiate into both Neu_02 and Neu_06, could the authors clarify
whether there is a significant preference in Neu_01 differentiation during the course
of immunotherapy combined with targeted therapy in RCC? In addition, the treatment
index highlights Neu_03 more prominently than Neu_06—why, then, was subsequent
analysis focused primarily on Neu_06? The authors are encouraged to clarify these
points.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful review and the insightful
comments. The predictive index (Pi) and treatment index (Ti) analyzes provided
complementary evidence supporting the functional relevance of neutrophil
heterogeneity in determining response to ICI plus TKI therapy in RCC (Results,
Lines 142-145). Specifically, the Pi analysis identified the Neu_01_S100A8 subset as
the neutrophil population most strongly associated with primary resistance,
underscoring its role as a critical upstream node within the neutrophil compartment.
Integrating Ti analysis with trajectory inference further revealed that therapeutic
response is not dictated by Neu_01 abundance per se, but rather by its differentiation
fate during treatment. In this context, an increase in Neu_06_VEGFA—arising from
Neu_01 along the resistance-associated trajectory—emerged as a key mediator of
treatment resistance, whereas alternative differentiation toward Neu_02 was
associated with favorable response (Fig. 2e). Collectively, these results indicate that
Neu_01 functions as a plastic progenitor-like state, with skewed differentiation
toward Neu_06 representing a dominant mechanism underlying resistance to ICI plus
TKI therapy in RCC.
2. Selection of CEACAM1 and LGALS3 as key markers of Neu_06
The authors state that CEACAM1 and LGALS3 are the two most characteristic
markers of Neu_06. However, in Figure 2b, the expression level of CEACAM1 does
not appear to be the highest compared with other molecules, such as LDHA or HK2,
which are strongly associated with anaerobic glycolysis. What is the rationale for
prioritizing CEACAM1 in the downstream analyses? Regarding LGALS3, the authors
note in line 150 that this molecule is broadly expressed in the tumor
microenvironment, yet it is not commonly reported in neutrophils. How do the authors
interpret the unusually high expression of LGALS3 within the Neu_06 subset, given
that this gene is not typically a canonical neutrophil marker? Clarification of this
apparent discrepancy would be helpful.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these important comments. The selection of
CEACAM1 and LGALS3 as characteristic markers of the Neu_06 subset was not based
solely on expression magnitude, but on a combination of subset specificity and
functional relevance to therapeutic resistance. Although glycolysis-associated genes
such as LDHA and HK2 are highly expressed in Neu_06, these molecules reflect a
general metabolic activation state shared across multiple cell types and lack
specificity for immune regulation. In contrast, CEACAM1 is preferentially expressed
in neutrophils and stromal cells and functions as a key immunomodulatory molecule
(Response Fig. 5). Its interaction with TIM-3 has been shown to promote T cell
dysfunction and immunosuppressive remodeling of the tumor microenvironment,
directly aligning with the resistance mechanisms investigated in this study. This
functional relevance motivated our prioritization of CEACAM1 for downstream
analyzes. With respect to LGALS3, we agree that it is broadly expressed in the tumor
microenvironment and is not a canonical neutrophil marker (Response Fig. 5).
However, LGALS3 can be induced in neutrophils under inflammatory or stress
conditions9. We interpret the elevated LGALS3 expression in Neu_06 as an acquired,
context-dependent phenotype associated with therapy-induced remodeling of the
TME, rather than a constitutive neutrophil lineage marker. We have revised the
manuscript to clarify these points and to better contextualize the biological
significance of CEACAM1 and LGALS3 in Neu_06 (Results, Lines 155-161) .
Response Fig. 5 Dot plot showing expression levels of marker genes (CEACAM1,
LGALS3 and HAVCR2) across major cell types. Dot size indicates the fraction of
expressing cells in each cluster, colored by normalized expression levels (now
Supplementary Fig. 3h in the revised manuscript).
3. Interpretation of CEACAM1 expression differences across datasets
In GSE243013 and GSE235863, CEACAM1 expression differs between response
groups, but these datasets consist of post-treatment specimens. Are these differences a
consequence of therapy (i.e., an adaptive or compensatory phenomenon), or do they
represent pre-existing molecular determinants that drive poor response? Would
pre-treatment specimens offer a more accurate reflection of the true driver
mechanisms underlying resistance? The authors are encouraged to clarify their
interpretation of these findings.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question regarding the
interpretation of CEACAM1 expression differences in the post-treatment datasets
GSE243013 and GSE235863. In GSE243013, we observed a higher proportion of
CEACAM1⁺ neutrophils in the post-treatment postNR group compared to responders
postR. Similarly, in the bulk RNA-seq dataset GSE235863, CEACAM1 gene
expression was significantly elevated in postNR samples. These consistent findings
across two independent cohorts suggest that sustained or induced CEACAM1
expression is associated with poor therapeutic response.
However, we fully acknowledge the reviewer’s important point because both
datasets consist of post-treatment specimens, it remains unclear whether elevated
CEACAM1 reflects a pre-existing resistance determinant or an adaptive/compensatory
response to therapy. Although we observed a trend toward higher abundance of
CEACAM1+ neutrophils in PreR compared to PreNR (Fig. 2i), the limited sample size
of pre-treatment cohorts prevents us from drawing definitive conclusions regarding
this difference. We agree that pre-treatment samples would be ideal for identifying
true driver mechanisms of resistance, and this limitation is now explicitly
acknowledged in the revised manuscript (Discussion, lines 451-456). Future studies
integrating longitudinal pre- and post-treatment samples will be essential to resolve
the causal direction of CEACAM1 upregulation.
Finally, we sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by unclear figure
labeling in the original submission. We have carefully revised the relevant figure
annotations (now Fig. 2i, 2k in the revised manuscript) to ensure accurate and
unambiguous presentation of the post-treatment group comparisons. We hope these
clarifications improve the interpretability of our findings.
4. Mechanistic interpretation of CEACAM1 and TIM-3 co-regulation
In Figure 4i, the authors report that CEACAM1 expression in neutrophils increases
compensatorily following Axitinib plus anti–PD-1 treatment, suggesting a link to
therapeutic resistance. Given that CEACAM1 and TIM-3 function as paired receptor–
ligand partners, the results imply that combined blockade of TIM-3 could potentially
broaden the responder population. However, numerous clinical trials combining PD-1
and TIM-3 inhibitors have yielded disappointing outcomes. Could the authors
reconcile this apparent contradiction between the preclinical observations and the
clinical reality? A more nuanced discussion of context-dependent mechanisms would
enhance the translational clarity of this section.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important and insightful comment. We
agree that the apparent discrepancy between our preclinical findings and the modest
efficacy of PD-1/TIM-3 combination therapies in clinical trials likely reflects strong
context dependency.
First, our data derive from patients who had developed resistance to PD-1–based
therapy. In this setting, we observed marked enrichment of CEACAM1+ neutrophils
and dominant TIM-3–mediated T cell dysfunction, suggesting that the CEACAM1–
TIM-3 axis becomes a key immunosuppressive pathway specifically in the post–PD-1
resistance context. Although we noted a trend toward higher CEACAM1+ neutrophil
abundance in pre-treatment responders (PreR) compared to non-responders (PreNR),
the limited size of pre-treatment cohorts precludes definitive conclusions about
baseline differences. Importantly, this implies that targeting CEACAM1–TIM-3 may
be most relevant for re-challenge or salvage strategies in PD-1–refractory disease,
rather than as a first-line intervention. In contrast, most completed PD-1/TIM-3
clinical trials enrolled treatment-naïve patients, where high response rates to standard
immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) may mask any incremental benefit of dual
blockade while increasing toxicity.
Second, TIM-3 signaling is modulated by multiple ligands including galectin-9,
HMGB1, phosphatidylserine, and CEACAM1 and operates within a network of
overlapping immunosuppressive circuits. Likewise, CEACAM1 engages other
receptors beyond TIM-3. Without stratification for neutrophil abundance, CEACAM1
expression, or myeloid-dominant immunosuppression, TIM-3 blockade alone may be
insufficient to overcome resistance in unselected patient populations.
Accordingly, we have revised the Discussion to clarify that our findings support
a context-specific role for the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis, providing a mechanistic
rationale for biomarker-guided re-challenge strategies in PD-1–refractory renal cell
carcinoma (RCC), rather than advocating its use as a universal first-line combination
(Discussion, Line 426-436). We believe this refined interpretation reconciles our
mechanistic observations with current clinical trial outcomes and underscores the
need for patient stratification based on myeloid features and CEACAM1 expression in
future studies.
Minor Concerns:
1. Line 193 – numbering error: In line 193, the numbering within “(5) EMT II (MP6;
SAA1, SAA2 and CXCL14), (6) MHC-II …” appears incorrect. Please revise the
numbering to maintain sequential consistency.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this numbering error. We have
corrected the sequence in the revised manuscript.
2. Figure 3d – definition of MP6: In Figure 3d, the boundary box highlighting MP6
(EMT-II) may not fully encompass all relevant regions, and there seems to be an
undefined area between MP6 and MP7. The authors are advised to recheck and clarify
the demarcation between these two modules to ensure accuracy.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have rechecked the
boundaries of MP6 and MP7 in Figure 3d and clarified the demarcation between the
two modules in both the figure and the legend to ensure accurate representation.
Briefly, the metaprograms (MPs) in our study were derived using Non-negative
Matrix Factorization (NMF) applied to single-cell transcriptomic data, followed by
module assignment based on gene set enrichment and inter-sample consistency
(Methods session). The Jaccard index is widely used to evaluate the similarity
between gene sets or biological modules, and its calculation is based on the
intersection and union of elements. During clustering, modules are formed by
aggregating gene sets that exhibit high Jaccard similarity.
However, we noticed that the gene sets corresponding to MP6 (EMT-II) and
MP7 show relatively low Jaccard similarity with each other. At the same time, a small
subset of gene signatures displays intermediate similarity to both modules, which
leads to the formation of an undefined area between them (Fig. 3d and Supplementary
Fig. 4a-4b). Importantly, this undefined area reflects the biological complexity of
TME remodeling rather than a technical artifact in module definition. We interpret
this phenomenon as a manifestation of the intricate TME dynamics induced by
combined PD-1 blockade and tyrosine kinase inhibition, which aligns with the
well-established heterogeneity and plasticity of aRCC10.
3. Figure 5a – potential inconsistency in CD8⁺ T-cell proportions: In Figure 5a, the
representative immunofluorescence images appear to show a higher proportion of
CD8⁺ T cells in the PT_Pre_NR group compared with PT_Post_R group, which
seems slightly inconsistent with the quantitative data presented in the statistical plot.
Please verify this point and ensure consistency between the visual and quantitative
results.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this observation. We have updated Fig. 5a to
ensure consistency between the representative immunofluorescence images and the
quantitative analysis.
4. Lines 309–316 – clarification of mechanistic reasoning: In lines 309–316, the
authors conclude that post-treatment resistance in RCC is attributed to the increased
proportion of PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺CD8⁺ T cells in the Post_NR group, implying that TIM-3
plays a pivotal role in mediating resistance to ICI + TKI therapy. However, this
conclusion logically depends on the premise that PD-1⁺ T cells are significantly
reduced after therapy. Although this reduction is observable in Figure 5c, the
manuscript would benefit from an explicit textual description emphasizing this key
observation to make the mechanistic reasoning more coherent and convincing.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. Our conclusion that
PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells contribute to resistance to ICI plus TKI therapy is based
on the observation that PD-1⁺ exhausted CD8⁺ T cells are markedly reduced after
treatment, particularly in non-responders. Although this reduction was evident in Fig.
5c, we agree that it was not sufficiently emphasized in the original text. Accordingly,
we have revised the Results section (Lines 312–317) to explicitly describe the
post-treatment decrease in PD-1⁺ CD8⁺ T cells and the concomitant enrichment of
PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for
implicating TIM-3 in acquired resistance.
5. Line 744 – correction of the formatting errors: The placement of the underline for
the link is incorrect. Please correct the placement of the underline for the link.
Response: We thank the reviewer for noticing this formatting issue. The underline for
the link in line 744 has been corrected in the revised manuscript.
6. Figure 6 – suggested addition for completeness: As the central conclusion of the
study revolves around the interaction among tumor cells, neutrophils, and T cells in
driving therapeutic resistance, it is recommended that the authors include in Figure 6 a
comparative analysis of mNeu_Ldha and mPd1–Tim3⁺Cd8⁺ T-cell populations across
different treatment groups following ML-T7 therapy. This addition would further
reinforce the integrative mechanistic framework proposed by the study.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we
performed a comparative analysis of Ceacam1+ neutrophils, Pd1+Tim3+ CD8+ T cells,
and Pd1-Tim3+ CD8+ T cells across distinct treatment groups, including control, anti–
PD-1 monotherapy, CEACAM1–TIM-3 blockade, and combination therapy.
First, combination therapy markedly reduced the proportion of Ceacam1+
neutrophils compared to all other groups (Response Fig. 6). In contrast, for Pd1-Tim3+
CD8+ T cells, the combination therapy increased their proportion compared to the
control group (Response Fig. 6).
Second, the proportion of Pd1+Tim3+ CD8+ T cells was elevated in all treatment
groups relative to the control group (Response Fig. 6). This finding suggests that
while combination therapy effectively targets myeloid-mediated immunosuppression,
it may not fully reverse or prevent the accumulation of highly exhausted CD8+ T cells
co-expressing both checkpoints. This incomplete reversal could be attributed to
persistent antigen exposure or compensatory feedback mechanisms within the tumor
microenvironment. Notably, compared with anti-PD-1 monotherapy, combination
therapy further downregulated the expression of multiple inhibitory immune
checkpoints including Pdcd1, Lag3, Havcr2, and Ctla4 on CD8+ T cells, indicating a
partial reversal of T cell exhaustion (Fig. 6h).
These findings highlight the dual-layered nature of the tumor immune response,
whereby effective modulation of the myeloid compartment does not automatically
translate into complete restoration of T cell functionality. We have now integrated
these results into Response Fig. 6 and expanded the accompanying text to discuss this
nuanced interplay (Lines 354-369). We believe this addition enriches the integrative
mechanistic framework of our study rather than simplifying it, by illustrating the
distinct dynamics of myeloid and lymphoid compartments under therapeutic pressure.
Response Fig. 6 Lollipop plots showing the proportion of Ceacam1+ neutrophils,
Pd1+Tim3+, and Pd1-Tim3+ CD8+ T cells in tumor samples from mice treated with
control, Toripalimab, ML-T7, or Toripalimab + ML-T7 as indicated (n = 2 per group;
total n = 8) (now Supplementary Fig. 10d in the revised manuscript).
By addressing these suggestions, the manuscript will be further strengthened in clarity
and completeness. Overall, this is an elegant, well-structured, and timely study that is
suitable for publication in Nature Communications after minor revisions to improve
clarity, figure presentation, and some text details.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive and encouraging comments. We
have carefully addressed all specific suggestions, clarified the methodology, refined
the figures, and polished the text. We believe these revisions further improve the
clarity, completeness, and overall presentation of the manuscript.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The combination of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has improved clinical outcomes in advanced renal cell carcinoma (aRCC), though therapeutic resistance remains a major challenge. We conducted single-cell transcriptomic analysis on 61 tumor samples from 34 aRCC patients treated with TKIs alone or in combination with ICIs. Non-responders exhibited increased neutrophil infiltration and enrichment of SAA+ tumor cells following treatment. We identified a VEGFA+CEACAM1+ neutrophil subset exhibiting immunosuppressive properties that is associated with poor clinical response. In vivo, pharmacologic inhibition of SAA enhanced sensitivity to ICI plus TKI combination therapy, while blockade of the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis in humanized PD-1 mouse models significantly potentiated anti–PD-1 efficacy. Our study establishes a single-cell atlas of the aRCC tumor microenvironment under treatment pressure and identifies a previously unrecognized SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis driving drug resistance, highlighting potential targets to improve therapy efficacy.

---

## Introduction

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for approximately 2–3% of adult malignancies worldwide, with clear cell RCC (ccRCC) representing 70–80% of cases1. Around 30% of patients present with metastatic disease, and 20–40% of those with localized tumors experience recurrence post-nephrectomy2. Advanced RCC (aRCC) remains a lethal disease with a 5-year survival rate of only 11.7%3. The discovery of von Hippel–Lindau mutations and the central role of angiogenesis in ccRCC led to the establishment of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) as first-line therapy4. Meanwhile, the immune-rich and pro-inflammatory nature of ccRCC supports the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Recently, combination therapy with TKIs and ICIs has transformed aRCC treatment, achieving survival benefits in both advanced2 and neoadjuvant settings5.

However, drug resistance remains a major clinical challenge, with 5–20% of patients failing to respond to combination therapies2. Current clinical tools fail to reliably identify patients at risk of resistance. Traditional ICI biomarkers, including PD-L1, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability, have limited utility in ccRCC. Transcriptomic studies in aRCC have revealed molecular subtypes associated with differential response—such as effector T cell and angiogenic signatures—but these findings require further validation6. A deeper understanding of the dynamic, multifactorial mechanisms underlying resistance, particularly the complex cellular crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment (TME), is essential for precision intervention. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers an unprecedented opportunity to dissect TME heterogeneity and track treatment-induced changes across cell types. Yet, an integrated single-cell–level analysis of resistance mechanisms in aRCC is lacking.

Here, we conduct comprehensive scRNA-seq analyses on 61 tumor samples from 34 aRCC patients treated with TKIs alone or in combination with ICIs. Our analyses reveal a previously unrecognized SAA⁺ tumor–CEACAM1+ neutrophil–CD8+ T cell axis that promotes immune suppression and therapeutic resistance. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for treatment failure and nominate actionable targets to overcome resistance in aRCC.

---

## Results

TME dynamics before and after ICI plus TIKI combination therapy in aRCC
We performed scRNA-seq on tumor samples from 18 patients in the PLAGH cohort, including three treated with TKI monotherapy, and 15 with ICI plus TKI combination therapy. A total of 30 tumor samples were analyzed: nine were pre-treatment samples (six from non-responders [PreNR], three from responders [PreR]) and 21 post-treatment samples (17 from non-responders [PostNR], four from responders [PostR]). The samples were obtained from primary tumors (n = 17), tumor thrombi (n = 9), adrenal metastatic lesion (n = 1) or mixed tissue (n = 3). One post-treatment sample (P6) was excluded due to poor sequencing quality (Supplementary Datasets 1,2).

To improve the analytical robustness of our study, we integrated two publicly available scRNA-seq datasets of aRCC. The first (HRA004711)7, including tumor and adjacent normal tissues from four patients treated with TKI monotherapy and the second (GSE264586)8, included samples from 12 patients treated with combination therapy, encompassing both primary and metastatic sites (Fig. 1a). After integration, the samples were classified as PreNR (n = 17), PreR (n = 8), PostNR (n = 26), and PostR (n = 10). After quality control, we profiled 333,169 high-quality single cells and constructed a comprehensive aRCC atlas, capturing the dynamic transcriptomic landscape across treatment (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 1a). Unsupervised clustering identified nine major cell types (Supplementary Dataset 3): normal epithelial cells (n = 5,544; Supplementary Dataset 4), tumor cells (n = 91,451), T/NK cells (n = 92,929; Supplementary Dataset 5), B cells (n = 10,407; Supplementary Dataset 6), plasma cells (n = 4,508; Supplementary Dataset 6), monocytic cells (n = 78,895; Supplementary Dataset 7), neutrophils (n = 14,779; Supplementary Dataset 8), mast cells (n = 2,303; Supplementary Dataset 9), and stromal cells (n = 32,353; Supplementary Dataset 10), based on canonical marker genes (Supplementary Figs. 1b–i and ; Supplementary Datasets 3–10).

Clinical trials including KEYNOTE-426, CheckMate 9ER, and RENOTORCH have demonstrated the superior efficacy of ICI plus TKI combination therapy compared to TKI monotherapy2. We compared changes in the proportions of major immune cell populations before and after treatment under these two therapeutic strategies. Notably, T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, B cells, plasma cells, and neutrophils exhibited distinct shifts in abundance. Neutrophils decreased following TKI monotherapy but increased with combination therapy (Supplementary Fig. 2a). A similar pattern was also observed for B cells and plasma cells (Supplementary Fig. 2a). In contrast, NK cells increased after TKI monotherapy but declined with combination therapy (Supplementary Fig. 2a). T cells increased after both treatments, especially in the combination group (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Within this group, responders had greater T cell enrichment, while macrophages and neutrophils were more predominant in non-responders (Supplementary Figs. 2b, c). Notably, responders exhibited higher T cell infiltration and reduced infiltration of myeloid cells across both treatment regimens (Supplementary Figs. 2b, c).

To quantify associations between immune cell populations and treatment outcomes, we applied a predictive index (Pi) and therapeutic index (Ti) frameworks9. T cells had the highest Pi, while neutrophils had the lowest (Fig. 1c). This finding was supported by multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) staining, which revealed elevated neutrophil infiltration in the PreNR group (Fig. 1d). Across multiple RCC cohorts receiving ICI monotherapy, TKI monotherapy, or combination therapy, higher neutrophil signature scores were associated with shorter overall and progression-free survival (Supplementary Fig. 2d).

Ti analysis also associated B cells and plasma cells with favorable treatment responses, in line with previous studies10,11. Conversely, macrophages and neutrophils were consistently enriched in non-responders (Fig. 1c). Notably, macrophage enrichment in resistant RCC has been previously reported12. Neutrophils were also enriched in the PostNR group in our cohorts (Fig. 1d), and the same patterns were also observed when comparing major pathologic response (MPR) and non-MPR (NMPR) obtained from the post-treatment samples in the non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) dataset (Supplementary Figs. 2e–g).

In summary, our findings reveal significant alterations in the TME landscape of aRCC patients undergoing TKI monotherapy or ICI plus TKI combination therapy. Specifically, these results suggest the involvement of neutrophils, which may potentially contribute to therapeutic resistance in aRCC patients.

Distinct neutrophils confer resistance to TKI with or without ICI
Tumor-associated neutrophils have been linked to immunotherapy resistance, with higher infiltration predicting poorer survival13. A pan-cancer analysis also revealed substantial transcriptional heterogeneity among neutrophils14. We performed high-resolution profiling of intratumoral neutrophils and identified six transcriptionally distinct subclusters: Neu_01_S100A8, Neu_02_CD74, Neu_03_Stress, Neu_04_ZFP36L1, Neu_05_IRF1, and Neu_06_VEGFA (Fig. 1b, Fig. 2a, and Supplementary Fig. 1i). The Neu_01_S100A8 exhibited enrichment in chemotaxis-related pathways and high expression of S100A12 (Supplementary Fig. 1i, 3a–b), resembling previously characterized S100A12+ 14 and CD10+ALPL+ neutrophils15. The Neu_02_CD74 displayed elevated CD74 expression and enrichment in antigen presentation pathways (Supplementary Fig. 1i, 3a, b), consistent with the HLA-DR+CD74+ neutrophils associated with favorable prognosis and improved PD-1 response14. The Neu_05_IRF1 expressed the immune checkpoint molecule CD274 (Fig. 2b), aligning with the PD-L1+ TANs that suppress T cell cytotoxicity16 (Supplementary Fig. 1i, 3a, b). Notably, the Neu_06_VEGFA subcluster (VEGFA+ neutrophils) expressed high expression of VEGFA, CXCR4, and LDHA (Fig. 2b), with enrichment in glycolysis and hypoxia-related pathways, similar to the VEGFA+SPP1+ neutrophils linked to poor prognosis14 (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 3a). This subset also exhibited high CXCR4 expression (Fig. 2b), consistent with CXCR4hi neutrophils characterized by increased neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation and inflammatory cytokine production, accompanied by lactate-driven vascular remodeling17.

After treatment, responders exhibited reduced proportions of Neu_01_S100A8, Neu_06_VEGFA, Neu_04_ZFP36L1, Neu_05_IRF1, and Neu_03_Stress, but a higher proportion of Neu_02_CD74 than non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Notably, while Neu_06_VEGFA was enriched in responders prior to treatment, its expansion was predominantly observed in non-responders after treatment (Supplementary Fig. 3c). This post-treatment enrichment was further validated by mIHC (Fig. 2d). Trajectory analysis revealed two primary differentiation routes from Neu_01_S100A8 towards either Neu_02_CD74 or Neu_06_VEGFA. Neutrophils predominantly differentiated along the Neu_02_CD74 lineage in responders and the Neu_06_VEGFA lineage in non-responders (Supplementary Figs. 3d–g). Pi and Ti analyses further supported these observations, with Pi identifying Neu_01_S100A8 as a baseline predictor of poor response, and Ti highlighting Neu_06_VEGFA as a treatment-associated mediator of therapeutic resistance (Fig. 2e). To assess neutrophil reprogramming following therapy, we compared the transcriptional profiles between PostR and PostNR samples. Neutrophils from PostNR samples exhibited upregulation of immune checkpoints including carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecule 1 (CEACAM1), VSIG4 and CD300A (Fig. 2f, Supplementary Dataset 11), along with enrichment of pathways related to angiogenesis, neutrophil chemotaxis and negative regulation of T cell-mediated immunity (Fig. 2g). Among all neutrophil subclusters, Neu_06_VEGFA showed the highest expression of LGALS3 and CEACAM1 (Figs. 2b, h)—ligands for LAG-3 and TIM-3, respectively, which are predominantly expressed on CD8+ T cells18. LGALS3 is widely expressed in the TME, including normal epithelial cells, tumor cells, monocytes, macrophages and mast cells19 (Supplementary Fig. 3h), its elevated expression in the Neu_06 subset likely reflects an acquired, stress-induced phenotype rather than a canonical neutrophil lineage marker. In contrast, CEACAM1 is mainly expressed in neutrophils and endothelial cells and is a key component of NETs20,21 (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Fig. 3i), underscoring its subset specificity and immunomodulatory relevance in resistance-associated neutrophils.

Disruption of CEACAM1–TIM-3 interactions has been shown to enhance PD-1 efficacy22,23. Given these observations, we investigated the association of CEACAM1+ neutrophils with non-responsiveness. In our cohort and three additional pan-cancer datasets, including NSCLC and colorectal cancer (CRC), CEACAM1+ neutrophils were significantly enriched in the PostNR group (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Figs. 3j–m), a finding further validated by mIHC (Fig. 2j). Post-treatment bulk RNA-seq revealed elevated CEACAM1 expression in non-responders, suggesting its association with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with ICI plus TKI (Fig. 2k).

We identified distinct neutrophil subpopulations linked to resistance against both TKI monotherapy and ICI plus TKI therapy. Among them, Neu_06_VEGFA stood out as a key immunosuppressive subset, potentially mediating resistance through CEACAM1–driven immunomodulatory effects.

SAA+ tumor cells associated with resistance to TKI with or without ICI
Tumor cells, as central components of the TME, play a pivotal role in shaping immune responses. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that tumor-derived signals recruit neutrophils, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive niche that facilitates tumor progression and therapy resistance24. To investigate the source of neutrophil recruitment in aRCC, we reconstructed cellular interaction networks through ligand-receptor analysis. In non-responders with aRCC, monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells more frequently expressed the chemokines (CXCL2, CXCL3 and CXCL8) to recruit CXCR2+ neutrophils compared to those in responders (Fig. 3a). Notably, tumor cells from post-treatment non-responders exhibited increased expression of CXCL14, a chemokine known to recruit CXCR4+ neutrophils25 (Fig. 3a). This is consistent with the Neu_06_VEGFA enrichment seen in PostNR samples (Fig. 2d).

To compare the differences in the cellular states of malignant cells between postR and postNR groups, we directly compared malignant cells from these two groups treated with ICI plus TKI to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Dataset 12). Notably, ferroptosis-inhibiting genes like SLC7A11 were enriched in malignant cells from the postNR group (Fig. 3b). Their upregulation, driven by interleukin 6 via the JAK2–STAT3 pathway, was previously reported in patients with aRCC receiving TKI monotherapy7. Our data indicate that the same pathway is activated during combination therapy, potentially driving resistance in non-responders. DEGs were also significantly enriched in pathways associated with acute inflammatory response and neutrophil infiltration, including SAA1 and SAAS2 (Figs. 3b, c).

Dimensionality reduction clustering of aRCC malignant cells revealed substantial inter-patient heterogeneity (Fig. 1b). To identify conserved functional programs while minimizing transcriptional variability driven by gene dosage effects, we applied non-negative matrix factorization. This approach defined nine metaprograms (MPs) in malignant cells, which were subsequently annotated into eight functional modules based on signature genes and enriched pathways (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Figs. 4a, b and Supplementary Dataset 13). These modules corresponded to: (1) cell cycle (MP1; TOP2A and STMN1), (2) neuronal-like26 (MP2; NR2F2 and PTPRG), (3) chemokines regulation (MP3; CXCL1 and CXCL2), (4) Proximal tubule (MP4; NAT8 and SLC17A3), (5) epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT I, MP5; LOX, PLOD2 and TGM2), (6) EMT II (MP6; SAA1, SAA2 and CXCL14), (7) MHC-II (MLP7; CD74 and HLA-DPA1), and (8) stress response processes (MP8; HSP90AA1 and HSPA1A). Module similarity analysis between our aRCC cohort and a recent study of treatment-naive RCC27 revealed strong concordance, suggesting that the functional architecture of tumor programs is largely preserved following treatment (Supplementary Fig. 4b). External validation of these findings using the TCGA-KIRC cohort confirmed a significant association between the activity of MP1, MP4, MP5, and MP6 tumor cell signatures and both overall survival and progression-free survival in patients with ccRCC (Supplementary Fig. 4c).

We annotated MP5 and MP6 as EMT-related modules based on their strong enrichment for hypoxia and EMT pathways (Supplementary Fig. 4a). MP5 incorporates extracellular matrix (ECM)-mediating factors, including LOX, PLOD2, TGM2 and is enriched in functions related to ECM organization (Fig. 3d). Its expression was significantly elevated in post-treatment samples compared to pre-treatment ones and was notably higher in PreNR tumor cells than in PreR cells (Fig. 3e). Additionally, MP6 contains SAA1, SAA2, CXCL14, and is enriched in functions related to the acute phase response, neutrophil chemotaxis, and migration (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Tumor cell scoring across our dataset and external single-cell datasets showed that MP6 was significantly upregulated in PostNR samples compared to PostR (Fig. 3e).

To further investigate tumor cell-intrinsic drivers of drug resistance in aRCC, we intersected genes from the postNR-enriched MP6 module with those consistently upregulated in both postNR samples and TKI-resistant ccRCC cell lines (A-498 and 786-O), identifying SAA1 and SAA2 as shared candidates (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Datasets 14,15). Serum amyloid A (SAA, comprising the SAA1/SAA2 isoforms in humans) is rapidly induced during acute-phase inflammatory responses28, and has been implicated in immune suppression and RCC progression29-31. Transcriptomic data from patients with HCC receiving ICI plus TKI therapy revealed higher SAA expression in postNR versus postR samples (Fig. 3g), suggesting a broader role for SAA in mediating resistance across cancers. Moreover, we validated that high SAA expression was significantly associated with poor survival outcomes in five previously published pan-cancer ICI datasets (Fig. 3i, Supplementary Figs. 4d, e). To assess the clinical utility of SAA as a predictive biomarker for ICI plus TKI therapy, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based quantification of pre-treatment plasma samples and found significantly elevated circulating SAA levels in patients with preNR tumors (Fig. 3j). At the tissue level, mIHC revealed increased SAA+ tumor cell abundance not only in preNR compared to preR samples, but also in post-treatment samples relative to pre-treatment, suggesting that therapy may further amplify the SAA+ tumor cell population enriched in NR groups (Fig. 3h). This enrichment was further confirmed in postNR versus postR tumors by both mIHC and scRNA-seq analyses (Fig. 3h; Supplementary Fig. 4f).

Collectively, these findings suggest that SAA+ tumor cells may constitute a persistent, treatment-amplified resistance population in aRCC.

SAA blockade enhances the combination therapy efficacy
SAA has been demonstrated to induce PD-L1 expression in neutrophils via LDHA/STAT3-mediated glycolytic activation and oncostatin M release, thereby attenuating cytotoxic T cell function in HCC32. Our data revealed significant enrichment of SAA+ tumor cells and Neu_06_ VEGFA in PostNR tumors, suggesting a symbiotic regulatory dynamic between these cell types. To clarify the spatial relationship between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils, we divided TME into tumor core and margin (Supplementary Fig. 5a-f). In non-responders, SAA+ cells mainly localize in the core with a few scattered in the margin, where VEGFA⁺ neutrophils are enriched (Supplementary Fig. 5g-h). Co-localization index analysis showed non-responders have higher indices than responders, supporting their potential interaction in non-responders’ tumor margin (Supplementary Fig. 5i). Furthermore, cell–cell communication analysis revealed enhanced interactions between SAA+ tumor cells and Neu_06_VEGFA in PostNR samples (Supplementary Fig. 6a). To functionally validate the SAA–CEACAM1 axis, we performed an in vitro perturbation experiment showing that SAA stimulation upregulates CEACAM1 expression in neutrophils (Fig. 4a, b; Supplementary Fig. 6b). Given the symbiotic interaction between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of targeting this axis in RCC. In preclinical syngeneic orthotopic RCC mouse models, triple therapy combining anti-SAA1/2 antibody, axitinib, and anti–PD-1 antibody produced a synergistic antitumor effect (Figs. 4c, d), without causing notable toxicity and outperforming either anti–PD-1 plus axitinib or anti-SAA1/2 monotherapy (Fig. 4e). mIHC analysis demonstrated that triple therapy increased CD8+ T cell infiltration (Fig. 4f) and significantly reduced neutrophil infiltration (Fig. 4g).

ScRNA-seq re-analysis of Saa-/- and wild-type (WT) mice33, revealed 11 major cell types using canonical markers (Supplementary Figs. 6c, d). Focusing on neutrophils, we identified eight distinct subpopulations (Supplementary Figs. 6e, f). Among them, mNeu_07_Ldha demonstrated notably higher expression levels of both Ldha and Hilpda and exhibited a transcriptional pattern highly comparable to that of Neu_06_VEGFA (Supplementary Fig. 6f). A significantly higher proportion of mNeu_07_Ldha was observed in WT mice (Figs. 4h, i).

Neutrophils from WT mice exhibited upregulation of angiogenesis- and chemotaxis-related genes and pathways (Fig. 4j, Supplementary Fig. 6g). Moreover, CD8+ T cells from Saa-/- mice exhibited enrichment in NK cell activation and immune-stimulatory pathways (Supplementary Fig. 6h). A comparison of transcriptomic differences between Saa-/- and WT neutrophils revealed upregulation of Ceacam1 expression (Fig. 4j). Similarly, SAA blockade using an anti-SAA1/2 antibody led to elevated Ceacam1 expression in neutrophils within the orthotopic RCC model (Fig. 4k).

Collectively, SAA+ tumor cells orchestrate a pro-tumor microenvironment by promoting Neu_06_VEGFA infiltration and CD8+ T cell dysfunction.

Diverse T cells distinguish therapy sensitivity and resistance
Numerous studies have underscored the importance of T cell characteristics within the TME and their influence on the response to anti-tumor therapies34. Our mIHC data revealed increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells in the PostR group following combination therapy (Fig. 5a). Conversely, a higher density of CD8+ T cells was observed in the PreNR group prior to treatment (Fig. 5a). This observation aligns with our previous report, in which biopsy specimens from non-responders exhibited enhanced infiltration of CD8+ cells5. Combination therapy also significantly enhanced T cell-mediated anti-tumor response activity in CD8+ T cells compared to TKI monotherapy (Supplementary Figs. 7a, b). Using high-resolution T/NK cell profiling in aRCC tumors, we identified four CD4+ T cell subsets, six CD8+ T cell subsets, and two NK cell subsets (Fig. 1b; Supplementary Figs. 1d, 7c and d). The CD8+ T cells were further classified into six subsets: cycling CD8+ T cells (CD8T_06_Cycling, MKI67+), memory-like CD8+ T cells (CD8T_01_CXCR4_preEX, TCF7+CCR7+CXCR4+), intermediate exhausted CD8+ T cells (CD8T_03_CCL5_Temra, GZMK+CCL5+CD74+, Exh-Pre), stress-state CD8+ T cells (CD8T_02_Stress, HSPA1A+, Exh-Prog), and two terminally exhausted subsets (CD8T_04_HAVCR2_EX, CCL5+ENTPDE1+HAVCR2+; Exh-Term and CD8T_05_CCL4_EX, CCL4+CCL4L2+CCL5+, Exh-KLR) (Figs. 1b, 5b; Supplementary Figs. 1d, 7e and f)35-37. Trajectory and proportion analyses indicated that, compared to TKI monotherapy, combination therapy appeared to facilitate the transition from Exh-Pre to Exh-Prog (Supplementary Figs. 7g-j). However, in the PostNR group receiving combination therapy, Exh-Prog cells accumulated, suggesting a potential blockade in their progression to terminally exhausted states (Supplementary Fig. 7h). This finding is consistent with the previously described significant enrichment of the terminally exhausted gene signature in cells from responders compared to non-responders in RCC immunotherapy35,38. The CD4+ T cells were reclustered into four subsets: naive CD4+ T cells (CD4T_01_Tn_CCR7, CCR7+), stress-state CD4+ T cells (CD4T_02_Stress, HSPA1A+), memory CD4+ T cells (CD4T_03_Tm_ANXA1, ANXA1+ CD40LG+), and regulatory T cells (Tregs, CD4T_04_Treg_FOXP3, FOXP3+) (Supplementary Figs. 1d, 7c and d). Compared to TKI monotherapy, combination therapy significantly increased the proportion of Tregs, particularly in the PostNR group (Supplementary Figs. 8a, b).

Previous studies have implicated TIM-3 and other immune checkpoints in adaptive resistance to PD-1 blockade39. Building on our findings of CEACAM1 enrichment in neutrophils from PostNR tumors, we noted that its ligand, TIM-3 (HAVCR2), is predominantly expressed on CD8+ T cells23, prompting investigation of the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis as a potential mediator of resistance. Across both therapeutic regimens, PD-1-TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells were significantly enriched in PostNR samples (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 9a and Supplementary Datasets 16,17). This finding was validated in three independent pan-cancer datasets (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Figs. 9b, c). PD-1-TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells exhibited elevated exhaustion scores (second only to PD-1+TIM-3+ cells) and reduced PD-1 response signatures (Supplementary Figs. 9d, e). Consistent with the reduction of PD-1+CD8+ T cells after treatment, the relative enrichment of PD-1-TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells suggests that TIM-3 upregulation, rather than sustained PD-1 signaling, represents the dominant exhaustion pathway in PostNR samples (Fig. 5c). Transcriptomic and pathway enrichment analyses demonstrated that TIM-3 upregulation was associated with enhanced immune evasion programs (Supplementary Figs. 9f-i) indicating a functional role for TIM-3 in adaptive resistance to PD-1 blockade.

Notably, spatial transcriptome-based cell abundance analysis revealed the co-occurrence of Neu_06_VEGFA and CD8⁺ T cell subsets (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 10a). Specifically, Neu_06_VEGFA and PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells exhibited spatial co-localization across multiple samples (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 10a). Intriguingly, in PostNR samples, Neu_06_VEGFA cells were positioned significantly closer to PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells than in PostR samples (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 10a). This observation was further supported by a higher co-localization index between these two populations in PostNR samples (Supplementary Fig. 10b), indicating a preferential spatial association of Neu_06_VEGFA with PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells in non-responders. Considering the limitations of low-resolution in Visium spot-level data, we further analyzed scRNA-seq data and found enhanced interactions between Neu_06_VEGSFA and PD-1- TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells (Figs. 5f, g). NicheNet analysis indicated that Neu_06_VEGFA may promote exhaustion in PD-1-TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells by upregulating the expression of exhaustion-associated transcription factors BHLHE40, PRDM1, and STAT3 via CEACAM1-HAVCR2 signaling (Fig. 5h).

In summary, combination therapy enhances CD8+ T cell infiltration but also accelerates their progressive exhaustion, especially in non-responders. The accumulation of Tregs and Exh-Prog CD8+ T cells fosters a more immunosuppressive TME following combination therapy. Our results indicate that the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis serves as a crucial driver of adaptive resistance, providing a potential therapeutic target to improve treatment efficacy.

CEACAM1–TIM-3 blockade alleviates anti–PD-1 resistance
CEACAM1 mediates immune evasion during the precancerous stage of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) via TIM-3 binding, and that TIM-3 blockade can attenuate tumor progression40. Notably, the anti-CEACAM1 monoclonal antibody exhibits synergistic anti-tumor activity with anti–PD-1 in NSCLC41, aligning with reports that disrupting CEACAM1–TIM-3 interactions enhances the efficacy of PD-1 blockade22,23. To evaluate the therapeutic potential of this axis, we utilized a humanized PD-1 mouse model bearing orthotopic murine RCC tumors, which inherently display resistance to PD-1 monotherapy42. ML-T7, a CEACAM1–TIM-3 blocking agent43, effectively suppressed tumor growth both as monotherapy and in combination with the human anti–PD-1 antibody Toripalimab (Figs. 6a–c). While Toripalimab monotherapy alone had no effect on tumor regression, the combination therapy achieved superior tumor control, with no significant weight loss, indicating a favorable safety profile (Figs. 6a–c). These findings are in line with previous studies in liver cancer, which showed that blockade of the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis enhances the efficacy of PD-1 inhibition22.

To explore the mechanism by which TIM-3 blockade overcomes PD-1 resistance in RCC, we conducted 10x GEM-X single-cell transcriptomic profiling on tumors harvested from mouse specimens (Fig. 6a). Unsupervised clustering identified 12 major cell types (Fig. 6d, Supplementary Fig. 10c and Supplementary Dataset 18). ML-T7 plus Toripalimab markedly reduced the proportion of Ceacam1+ neutrophils compared to all other groups (Supplementary Fig. 10d), while increasing the proportion of Pd-1-Tim-3+ CD8+ T cells relative to the control group (Supplementary Fig. 10d). In contrast, PD-1+TIM-3+ CD8+ T cells were elevated in all treatment groups compared to the control (Supplementary Fig. 10d). This finding suggests that while combination therapy effectively targets myeloid-mediated immunosuppression, it does not fully prevent the accumulation of highly exhausted CD8+ T cells co-expressing both checkpoints. Interestingly, differential abundance analysis revealed a significant enrichment of macrophages in the ML-T7 plus Toripalimab group compared to the control group, while neutrophils were predominantly enriched in the control group (Figs. 6e, f). Notably, the ML-T7 monotherapy group displayed a similar macrophage enrichment pattern to that of the combination therapy (Supplementary Fig. 10e, f). In contrast, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and NK cells were more abundant in the control group relative to ML-T7 monotherapy (Supplementary Figs. 10e, f). Toripalimab monotherapy resulted in enrichment of CD4+, CD8+, and NK cells, as well as neutrophils, while showing macrophage infiltration patterns comparable to those of the control (Supplementary Figs. 10g, h).

To further investigate the effect of TIM-3 blockade on CD8+ T cells, we compared exhaustion, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and mitochondrial organization scores across treatment groups. CD8+ T cells from the ML-T7 plus Toripalimab group exhibited significantly lower exhaustion and tolerance scores but higher OXPHOS and mitochondrial function scores than other groups (Fig. 6g), consistent with the known metabolic rewiring during T cell activation44. In contrast, Toripalimab monotherapy exhibited the highest exhaustion scores and upregulation of checkpoint genes like Havcr2 and transcription factors such as Stat3 and Entpd1 (Fig. 6h). The combination treatment was enriched for mitochondrial metabolism genes including Tpi1 and Fabp5 (Fig. 6h).

Our results aslo showed that ML-T7 combined with Toripalimab markedly increased macrophage abundance (Figs. 6e, f). Further analysis revealed that macrophages from the combination group exhibited marked downregulation of genes associated with NLRP3 inflammasome activation relative to controls (Fig. 6i), accompanied by downregulation of key inflammasome genes such as Nlrp3, Il1a, and Il1b (Fig. 6j). These data are consistent with accumulating evidence that macrophage-intrinsic NLRP3 inflammasome activation drives tumor progression and undermines immunotherapeutic efficacy45.

Collectively, the ML-T7 plus anti–PD-1 combination may overcome resistance by reinvigorating CD8+ T cells and reducing myeloid-driven immunosuppression through inhibition of macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activity.
