Reviewer #2 :
Gu et al. present a well-executed study that combines single-cell and spatial
transcriptomic analyses to dissect the immune-tumor interactions underlying
therapeutic resistance in advanced aRCC. The integration of multi-omics data with
clinical response information and experimental validation is impressive, and the work
provides mechanistic insights with relatively clear translational relevance. The
identification of the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 axis as a driver of immunosuppressive
TME and therapy resistance may open new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the encouraging comments and recognition of
our multi-omics integration and mechanistic findings. We appreciate the positive
assessment of the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis and its translational relevance. We
have revised the manuscript to further clarify key methodological details and improve
the presentation. We also added new in-vitro data supporting the direct effect of
SAA-stimulated neutrophils on CEACAM1 upregulation, which strengthens the
proposed mechanism. We are grateful for the reviewer’s constructive feedback.
Major Comments:
1. The manuscript identifies the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 axis as a potential
mechanistic pathway contributing to resistance to TKI plus ICI therapy. However,
much of this mechanistic link remains inferred from transcriptomic correlations and
ligand-receptor analyses. Although the authors demonstrate that SAA inhibition
enhances therapeutic efficacy in a mouse model, direct functional validation of the
key molecular players (e.g., SAA1/2, CEACAM1, and TIM-3) would greatly
strengthen the mechanistic claims, even just in cell-based systems. For example,
knockdown or overexpression studies in RCC cell lines, neutrophil co-culture assays,
or cytokine signaling blockade experiments could directly test the causality of these
interactions. At minimum, perturbation experiments in vitro would reinforce the
conclusion that this axis is mechanistically responsible for the observed phenotypes
rather than merely correlative.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In the revised
manuscript, we added a direct in vitro functional perturbation experiment
demonstrating that SAA stimulation upregulates CEACAM1 expression in neutrophils
(Response Fig. 2), providing functional evidence for the proposed SAA–CEACAM1
axis. In these experiments, neutrophils were freshly isolated from peripheral blood of
treatment-naïve RCC patients using CD15 magnetic bead–based separation (>99%
purity) and subsequently stimulated with recombinant human SAA protein.
To extend these findings in vivo, SAA inhibition reduced neutrophil infiltration
and enhanced the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in an RCC mouse model (Fig. 4d, g).
Importantly, mIHC analysis of clinical samples further validated these observations,
revealing a significantly higher proportion of CEACAM1+ neutrophils in
non-responders compared with responders (Fig. 2j), supporting the clinical relevance
of CEACAM1 upregulation in therapeutic resistance.
Moreover, the CEACAM1–TIM-3 interaction has been well established in prior
studies³⁻⁴, providing additional mechanistic support. Collectively, these
complementary in vitro, in vivo, and patient-derived data strengthen the causal link
between the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis and the establishment of an
immunosuppressive TME, ultimately driving resistance to TKI plus ICI therapy.
Regarding the reviewer’s suggestion for genetic perturbation experiments, we
note that the short lifespan and limited transfectability of primary neutrophils make
direct SAA knockdown technically challenging. Therefore, we employed recombinant
SAA protein to model its biological effects, an approach that is physiologically
relevant given that SAA functions as a secreted acute-phase protein.
Response Fig. 2 SAA stimulation upregulates CEACAM1 expression in RCC
patients’ neutrophils. (a) Representative flow cytometry histograms showing surface
CD66a/c/e expression in human neutrophils following stimulation with increasing
concentrations of recombinant human SAA (0, 250, 500, and 1,000 ng/mL) for 12
hours (now Fig. 4a in the revised manuscript). (b) Quantification of relative
CEACAM1 expression levels assessed by flow cytometry (left) and qRT-PCR (right)
under the indicated SAA concentrations. Each dot represents an independent sample
(n = 8). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. P values were calculated using an
unpaired two-sided t-test (now Fig. 4b in the revised manuscript). (c) Flow
cytometric gating strategy demonstrates efficient enrichment of CD15⁺ neutrophils
(>99% purity) following magnetic separation. Sequential gating excluded debris and
doublets prior to assessment of CD15 and CD66a/c/e expression (now
Supplementary Fig. 6b in the revised manuscript).
2. The manuscript reports several mechanistic findings involving SAA+ tumor cells,
VEGFA+ neutrophils, Tregs, CEACAM1-TIM-3 signaling, and angiogenesis. While
each of these findings is biologically meaningful, presenting them all in equal detail
makes the narrative somewhat diffuse. The authors may consider prioritizing one
central mechanism, such as the SAA-CEACAM1-TIM-3 immunoregulatory loop, as
the main storyline, while condensing or relocating secondary mechanisms (e.g., Treg
involvement, VEGFA signaling). This refinement would sharpen the mechanistic
focus and help readers appreciate the central conceptual advance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion, which has
significantly helped refine the clarity of our mechanistic narrative. In the revised
manuscript, we have restructured the narrative to center on the SAA–CEACAM1–
TIM-3 immunoregulatory loop as the primary mechanistic axis driving
immunotherapy resistance in aRCC. To sharpen the mechanistic focus, content
describing secondary mechanisms including Treg infiltration, VEGFA+ neutrophil
mediated angiogenesis has been streamlined and concisely integrated into the main
Results section (Line 242-251, 300-302) . Through this revision, we aim to provide a
more focused and coherent narrative that enables readers to readily grasp the central
mechanistic insight of our study.
3. The spatial transcriptomic analyses provide valuable contextual information, but
the spatial localization of the SAA+ tumor regions relative to VEGFA+ neutrophils
and CD8+ T cells could be presented more quantitatively. Strengthening the link
between spatial proximity and inferred signaling axes, for instance, through
co-localization metrics or neighborhood enrichment analyses, would provide stronger
evidence for spatially coordinated immunoregulation. This integration would also
guide selection of targetable microenvironmental niches for future therapeutic
exploration.
Response: We thank the reviewer for giving us suggestions on how to improve our
work. We agree that a more quantitative spatial analysis would strengthen the link
between tumor-derived SAA and its immunomodulatory effects on VEGFA+
neutrophils and CD8+ T cells. We have carefully addressed this concern
through supplementary quantitative spatial analyzes, and the detailed revisions are
summarized below:
1. Spatial localization characteristics between SAA+ tumor regions
and VEGFA+ neutrophils
To clarify the spatial relationship between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils,
we stratified the TME into two distinct compartments including tumor core and tumor
margin. We observed distinct spatial distributions of SAA+ tumor cells between
responders and non-responders based on the deconvolution results generated by the
spotiphy algorithm. Notably, in non-responders, SAA+ tumor cells were predominantly
localized within the tumor core, with only a minor subset scattered in the tumor
margin (Response Fig. 3a). In contrast, VEGFA+ neutrophils are significantly enriched
in the tumor margin (Response Fig. 3b), a spatial domain that overlaps with the
distribution of these scattered SAA⁺ tumor cells (Response Fig. 3b).
Given that SAA is a secreted protein, we hypothesize that SAA produced by
tumor cells within the tumor core diffuses to the tumor margin and exerts paracrine
effects on VEGFA+ neutrophils. Supporting this model, the mIHC showed that both
VEGFA+ neutrophils (Fig. 2d) and SAA+ tumor cells (Fig. 3h) are significantly more
abundant in non-responders compared to responders after treatment, suggesting a
potential SAA–neutrophil axis in non-responders. Critically, our in vitro experiments
demonstrated that recombinant SAA significantly upregulates CEACAM1 expression
in RCC patients’s neutrophils (Response Fig. 2), indicating that tumor-derived SAA
can modulate neutrophil function independently of direct cell–cell contact.
Unexpectedly, the presence of scattered SAA+ tumor cells in the tumor margin
prompted us to further explore their potential interaction with VEGFA+ neutrophils,
particularly in non-responder patients. To test this hypothesis, we computed a
co-localization index between SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils specifically
within the tumor margin, following a previously described analytical pipeline3.
Notably, our data demonstrated that non-responders (STpost3 and STpost4) exhibit
significantly higher co-localization indices compared to responders (STpost1 and
STpost2). This finding supports the potential interaction between SAA⁺ malignant
cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils in the tumor margin of non-responders. Comparative
analysis further revealed that patient STpost4 exhibited the highest co-localization
index among all patients (Response Fig. 3c). Importantly, clinical follow-up data
showed that STpost4 subsequently experienced tumor recurrence, suggesting that this
spatial co-localization may not only be associated with resistance to ICI plus TKI
combination therapy but also with disease progression (Supplementary Table 1).
Response Fig. 3 Spatial distribution of SAA+ tumor cells and VEGFA+ neutrophils.
(a-b) Boxplots showing the proportion of SAA+ tumor cells (a) and VEGFA+
neutrophils (b) across distinct tissue regions (tumor core vs. tumor margin) in four
patients. (c) Boxplots comparing the co-localization index between SAA+ tumor cells
and VEGFA+ neutrophils in the tumor margin across four patients. P values were
calculated using unpaired two-sided t-test. In all boxplots, the center line in the
boxplots indicates the median, the lower and upper hinges correspond to the first and
third quartiles, and the whiskers extend at most 1.5 times the interquartile range past
the upper and lower quartiles (Now Supplementary Fig. 5g-i in the revised
manuscript).
2. Quantitative analysis of spatial distance between CD8+ T cells
and VEGFA+ neutrophils
To further strengthen the characterization of the spatial regulatory network in TME,
we performed quantitative cell-cell distance measurement analysis focusing on
CD8+ T cells subsets and VEGFA+ neutrophils. To quantitatively assess the spatial
relationships between these cell subsets, we applied Kullback-Leibler (KL)
divergence analysis4,5. Density plots consistently revealed that VEGFA+ neutrophils
exhibited greater spatial similarity and pronounced co-localization with three CD8+ T
cells subsets (PD-1-TIM-3+, PD-1+TIM-3+, PD-1-TIM-3-), which was reflected by
lower KL divergence values (Response Fig. 4a-d). Notably, among all non-responder
patients (STpost3 and STpost4), the KL divergence values between VEGFA+
neutrophils and the three aforementioned CD8+ T cell subsets were below 2
(Response Fig. 4a-b). In contrast, higher KL divergence values were observed
between these cell populations in another responder sample (STpost2) (Response Fig.
4c). For STpost1, due to the extremely low proportion of VEGFA+ neutrophils
(Response Fig. 3b) obtained via deconvolution, co-localization analysis between
VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cells was not performed for this sample. We have
provided more details in the Methods session “Cell type co-localization analysis” in
the revised manuscript.
Response Fig. 4 Spatial co-localization between VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cell
subsets. (a-c) Spatial mapping of cell types onto spatial transcriptomics (ST) slides
from three post-treatment samples STpost3 (a), STpost4 (b), and STpost2 (c) using
the spotiphy deconvolution method. Color intensity represents estimated relative
abundance for all cell types (top left) and individual cell type (top right). The density
plots display the KL divergence of the observed co-localization pattern relative to a
null distribution derived from spatial permutation (bottom). (d) Boxplots comparing
the co-localization index between VEGFA+ neutrophils and CD8+ T cell subsets
indicated in the tumor margin across three patients. P values were calculated using
two-sided Student’s t-test. In all boxplots, the center line in the boxplots indicates the
median, the lower and upper hinges correspond to the first and third quartiles, and the
whiskers extend at most 1.5 times the interquartile range past the upper and lower
quartiles (Now Fig.5e, Supplementary Fig. 10a, b in the revised manuscript)..
4. To further enhance the translational potential of the study, it would be beneficial to
discuss strategies for dual targeting of SAA and CEACAM1, given their
compensatory relationship. A clear statement on how these preclinical findings may
inform patient stratification or biomarker development in RCC would also strengthen
clinical relevance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the translational potential of
targeting SAA and CEACAM1, a point also raised by Reviewer #1. In response, we
have expanded the Discussion (Line 403-450) to explicitly address the translational
implications of these findings, including therapeutic strategies, patient stratification,
and biomarker development.
As now discussed, although SAA and CEACAM1 exhibit a compensatory
relationship, their druggability differs substantially. SAA, as a secreted acute-phase
protein, is less tractable as a direct therapeutic target, whereas CEACAM1 is a
membrane-bound receptor with higher target specificity. Consequently, simultaneous
dual targeting may be challenging in practice. Nevertheless, SAA remains a promising
predictive biomarker for immunotherapy response (Fig. 3j) and multiple independent
studies, including recent evidence in hepatocellular carcinoma6,7. We also
acknowledge that the current sample size for SAA-based analyzes is limited, and that
validation in larger, independent cohorts will be required to firmly establish its
predictive value and clinical applicability.
From a therapeutic perspective, our findings suggest a potential stratified
approach: SAA may serve as a biomarker to identify patients at risk of primary
resistance, while CEACAM1 represents a more actionable target for patients with
immune-refractory disease. In this context, re-challenge strategies targeting
CEACAM1 are conceptually supported by existing phase II clinical data on CM248.
Although CEACAM1-directed antibodies are not yet clinically available in China, we
are currently pursuing translational development through collaboration with a
domestic pharmaceutical partner (Junshi Biosciences Co., Ltd.) to advance
CEACAM1-targeted therapeutic strategies. Additional preclinical validation studies
are ongoing, and detailed data cannot be disclosed at this stage due to confidentiality
considerations.
Reviewer #3:
This study was conducted using clinical trial specimens together with public datasets
and focuses on the core challenge of resistance to combined immune-targeted therapy
in renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Through single-cell sequencing and humanized mouse
models, the authors propose a novel mechanism whereby tumor cell–neutrophil
interactions can mediate the resistance of immunotherapy combined with targeted
therapy in RCC.
Fit with Nature Communications: Nature Communications values mechanistic
discoveries that bridge fundamental biological understanding with clinical translation.
This study exemplifies that mission by beginning with clinically validated phenomena,
applying state-of-the-art single-cell technologies to interrogate the biological “black
box,” and completing the translational exploration preliminarily through further
validation in humanized mouse models. The conceptual design—spanning from
clinical observation to mechanistic exploration and translational
confirmation—closely aligns with the journal’s aim to publish conceptually
innovative and broadly relevant biomedical research.
Novel Mechanistic Point: The study reveals that VEGFA⁺ neutrophils (Neu_06) are
enriched in non-responders and specifically interact with SAA⁺ tumor cells. This
interaction promotes T-cell exhaustion through the CEACAM1–TIM3 ligand–
receptor axis, thereby establishing a new mechanistic framework linking metabolic
reprogramming in myeloid cells to adaptive immune dysfunction. Such a finding
provides an original and well-supported explanation for resistance to immunotherapy
combined with targeted therapy in RCC.
Translational Value: Using RCC samples from patients with distinct efficacy and
some public datasets, the study identifies actionable pathways driving resistance. The
demonstration that inhibition of SAA in Balb/c mice or pharmacologic blockade of
CEACAM1–TIM3 signaling in humanized mouse models can both enhance treatment
efficacy, which confers strong translational value. These results not only support
biomarker-based patient stratification but also propose combination therapeutic
strategies with the potential to improve outcomes in patients who are super-resistant
to current immunotherapies—a population with critical unmet clinical needs.
I recommend Minor Revision for this manuscript. The study is robust overall, but a
few targeted refinements are needed to maximize its clarity and impact prior to
acceptance. The required revisions are primarily clarifications and minor additional
analyses; no fundamental flaws are present. Addressing the points below will ensure
the manuscript achieves its full potential for a high-impact venue.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thorough and encouraging assessment of our
study and for recommending Minor Revisions. We appreciate the recognition of our
integrated approach combining clinical samples, public datasets, single-cell analyzes,
and humanized mouse models to uncover the SAA–CEACAM1–TIM-3–mediated
mechanism of immunotherapy resistance in RCC. In response, we have clarified
methodological details, emphasized the central mechanistic storyline, slightly
extended the mechanistic discussion, and polished the presentation. We believe these
revisions further strengthen the clarity, rigor, and overall impact of the manuscript for
the Nature Communications readership.
Major Concerns:
1. Role and differentiation trajectory of neutrophils
Neutrophils are a critical component of the tumor microenvironment. In Figure 1c, the
predictive index indicates that baseline neutrophil abundance shows the strongest
negative correlation with response to ICI+TKI in RCC, thereby justifying the authors’
focus on neutrophil subclusters. The study further suggests that differentiation from
Neu_01 to Neu_02 mediates therapeutic response, while differentiation from Neu_01
to Neu_06 contributes to resistance. In Figure 2e, Neu_01 shows the most negative
correlation with efficacy in the predictive index, yet its dynamic change in the
treatment index is most positively correlated with therapeutic response. Given that
Neu_01 can differentiate into both Neu_02 and Neu_06, could the authors clarify
whether there is a significant preference in Neu_01 differentiation during the course
of immunotherapy combined with targeted therapy in RCC? In addition, the treatment
index highlights Neu_03 more prominently than Neu_06—why, then, was subsequent
analysis focused primarily on Neu_06? The authors are encouraged to clarify these
points.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful review and the insightful
comments. The predictive index (Pi) and treatment index (Ti) analyzes provided
complementary evidence supporting the functional relevance of neutrophil
heterogeneity in determining response to ICI plus TKI therapy in RCC (Results,
Lines 142-145). Specifically, the Pi analysis identified the Neu_01_S100A8 subset as
the neutrophil population most strongly associated with primary resistance,
underscoring its role as a critical upstream node within the neutrophil compartment.
Integrating Ti analysis with trajectory inference further revealed that therapeutic
response is not dictated by Neu_01 abundance per se, but rather by its differentiation
fate during treatment. In this context, an increase in Neu_06_VEGFA—arising from
Neu_01 along the resistance-associated trajectory—emerged as a key mediator of
treatment resistance, whereas alternative differentiation toward Neu_02 was
associated with favorable response (Fig. 2e). Collectively, these results indicate that
Neu_01 functions as a plastic progenitor-like state, with skewed differentiation
toward Neu_06 representing a dominant mechanism underlying resistance to ICI plus
TKI therapy in RCC.
2. Selection of CEACAM1 and LGALS3 as key markers of Neu_06
The authors state that CEACAM1 and LGALS3 are the two most characteristic
markers of Neu_06. However, in Figure 2b, the expression level of CEACAM1 does
not appear to be the highest compared with other molecules, such as LDHA or HK2,
which are strongly associated with anaerobic glycolysis. What is the rationale for
prioritizing CEACAM1 in the downstream analyses? Regarding LGALS3, the authors
note in line 150 that this molecule is broadly expressed in the tumor
microenvironment, yet it is not commonly reported in neutrophils. How do the authors
interpret the unusually high expression of LGALS3 within the Neu_06 subset, given
that this gene is not typically a canonical neutrophil marker? Clarification of this
apparent discrepancy would be helpful.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these important comments. The selection of
CEACAM1 and LGALS3 as characteristic markers of the Neu_06 subset was not based
solely on expression magnitude, but on a combination of subset specificity and
functional relevance to therapeutic resistance. Although glycolysis-associated genes
such as LDHA and HK2 are highly expressed in Neu_06, these molecules reflect a
general metabolic activation state shared across multiple cell types and lack
specificity for immune regulation. In contrast, CEACAM1 is preferentially expressed
in neutrophils and stromal cells and functions as a key immunomodulatory molecule
(Response Fig. 5). Its interaction with TIM-3 has been shown to promote T cell
dysfunction and immunosuppressive remodeling of the tumor microenvironment,
directly aligning with the resistance mechanisms investigated in this study. This
functional relevance motivated our prioritization of CEACAM1 for downstream
analyzes. With respect to LGALS3, we agree that it is broadly expressed in the tumor
microenvironment and is not a canonical neutrophil marker (Response Fig. 5).
However, LGALS3 can be induced in neutrophils under inflammatory or stress
conditions9. We interpret the elevated LGALS3 expression in Neu_06 as an acquired,
context-dependent phenotype associated with therapy-induced remodeling of the
TME, rather than a constitutive neutrophil lineage marker. We have revised the
manuscript to clarify these points and to better contextualize the biological
significance of CEACAM1 and LGALS3 in Neu_06 (Results, Lines 155-161) .
Response Fig. 5 Dot plot showing expression levels of marker genes (CEACAM1,
LGALS3 and HAVCR2) across major cell types. Dot size indicates the fraction of
expressing cells in each cluster, colored by normalized expression levels (now
Supplementary Fig. 3h in the revised manuscript).
3. Interpretation of CEACAM1 expression differences across datasets
In GSE243013 and GSE235863, CEACAM1 expression differs between response
groups, but these datasets consist of post-treatment specimens. Are these differences a
consequence of therapy (i.e., an adaptive or compensatory phenomenon), or do they
represent pre-existing molecular determinants that drive poor response? Would
pre-treatment specimens offer a more accurate reflection of the true driver
mechanisms underlying resistance? The authors are encouraged to clarify their
interpretation of these findings.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question regarding the
interpretation of CEACAM1 expression differences in the post-treatment datasets
GSE243013 and GSE235863. In GSE243013, we observed a higher proportion of
CEACAM1⁺ neutrophils in the post-treatment postNR group compared to responders
postR. Similarly, in the bulk RNA-seq dataset GSE235863, CEACAM1 gene
expression was significantly elevated in postNR samples. These consistent findings
across two independent cohorts suggest that sustained or induced CEACAM1
expression is associated with poor therapeutic response.
However, we fully acknowledge the reviewer’s important point because both
datasets consist of post-treatment specimens, it remains unclear whether elevated
CEACAM1 reflects a pre-existing resistance determinant or an adaptive/compensatory
response to therapy. Although we observed a trend toward higher abundance of
CEACAM1+ neutrophils in PreR compared to PreNR (Fig. 2i), the limited sample size
of pre-treatment cohorts prevents us from drawing definitive conclusions regarding
this difference. We agree that pre-treatment samples would be ideal for identifying
true driver mechanisms of resistance, and this limitation is now explicitly
acknowledged in the revised manuscript (Discussion, lines 451-456). Future studies
integrating longitudinal pre- and post-treatment samples will be essential to resolve
the causal direction of CEACAM1 upregulation.
Finally, we sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by unclear figure
labeling in the original submission. We have carefully revised the relevant figure
annotations (now Fig. 2i, 2k in the revised manuscript) to ensure accurate and
unambiguous presentation of the post-treatment group comparisons. We hope these
clarifications improve the interpretability of our findings.
4. Mechanistic interpretation of CEACAM1 and TIM-3 co-regulation
In Figure 4i, the authors report that CEACAM1 expression in neutrophils increases
compensatorily following Axitinib plus anti–PD-1 treatment, suggesting a link to
therapeutic resistance. Given that CEACAM1 and TIM-3 function as paired receptor–
ligand partners, the results imply that combined blockade of TIM-3 could potentially
broaden the responder population. However, numerous clinical trials combining PD-1
and TIM-3 inhibitors have yielded disappointing outcomes. Could the authors
reconcile this apparent contradiction between the preclinical observations and the
clinical reality? A more nuanced discussion of context-dependent mechanisms would
enhance the translational clarity of this section.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important and insightful comment. We
agree that the apparent discrepancy between our preclinical findings and the modest
efficacy of PD-1/TIM-3 combination therapies in clinical trials likely reflects strong
context dependency.
First, our data derive from patients who had developed resistance to PD-1–based
therapy. In this setting, we observed marked enrichment of CEACAM1+ neutrophils
and dominant TIM-3–mediated T cell dysfunction, suggesting that the CEACAM1–
TIM-3 axis becomes a key immunosuppressive pathway specifically in the post–PD-1
resistance context. Although we noted a trend toward higher CEACAM1+ neutrophil
abundance in pre-treatment responders (PreR) compared to non-responders (PreNR),
the limited size of pre-treatment cohorts precludes definitive conclusions about
baseline differences. Importantly, this implies that targeting CEACAM1–TIM-3 may
be most relevant for re-challenge or salvage strategies in PD-1–refractory disease,
rather than as a first-line intervention. In contrast, most completed PD-1/TIM-3
clinical trials enrolled treatment-naïve patients, where high response rates to standard
immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) may mask any incremental benefit of dual
blockade while increasing toxicity.
Second, TIM-3 signaling is modulated by multiple ligands including galectin-9,
HMGB1, phosphatidylserine, and CEACAM1 and operates within a network of
overlapping immunosuppressive circuits. Likewise, CEACAM1 engages other
receptors beyond TIM-3. Without stratification for neutrophil abundance, CEACAM1
expression, or myeloid-dominant immunosuppression, TIM-3 blockade alone may be
insufficient to overcome resistance in unselected patient populations.
Accordingly, we have revised the Discussion to clarify that our findings support
a context-specific role for the CEACAM1–TIM-3 axis, providing a mechanistic
rationale for biomarker-guided re-challenge strategies in PD-1–refractory renal cell
carcinoma (RCC), rather than advocating its use as a universal first-line combination
(Discussion, Line 426-436). We believe this refined interpretation reconciles our
mechanistic observations with current clinical trial outcomes and underscores the
need for patient stratification based on myeloid features and CEACAM1 expression in
future studies.

2. Figure 3d – definition of MP6: In Figure 3d, the boundary box highlighting MP6
(EMT-II) may not fully encompass all relevant regions, and there seems to be an
undefined area between MP6 and MP7. The authors are advised to recheck and clarify
the demarcation between these two modules to ensure accuracy.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have rechecked the
boundaries of MP6 and MP7 in Figure 3d and clarified the demarcation between the
two modules in both the figure and the legend to ensure accurate representation.
Briefly, the metaprograms (MPs) in our study were derived using Non-negative
Matrix Factorization (NMF) applied to single-cell transcriptomic data, followed by
module assignment based on gene set enrichment and inter-sample consistency
(Methods session). The Jaccard index is widely used to evaluate the similarity
between gene sets or biological modules, and its calculation is based on the
intersection and union of elements. During clustering, modules are formed by
aggregating gene sets that exhibit high Jaccard similarity.
However, we noticed that the gene sets corresponding to MP6 (EMT-II) and
MP7 show relatively low Jaccard similarity with each other. At the same time, a small
subset of gene signatures displays intermediate similarity to both modules, which
leads to the formation of an undefined area between them (Fig. 3d and Supplementary
Fig. 4a-4b). Importantly, this undefined area reflects the biological complexity of
TME remodeling rather than a technical artifact in module definition. We interpret
this phenomenon as a manifestation of the intricate TME dynamics induced by
combined PD-1 blockade and tyrosine kinase inhibition, which aligns with the
well-established heterogeneity and plasticity of aRCC10.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. Our conclusion that
PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells contribute to resistance to ICI plus TKI therapy is based

PD-1⁻TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺ T cells, thereby strengthening the mechanistic rationale for
implicating TIM-3 in acquired resistance.

6. Figure 6 – suggested addition for completeness: As the central conclusion of the

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we
performed a comparative analysis of Ceacam1+ neutrophils, Pd1+Tim3+ CD8+ T cells,
and Pd1-Tim3+ CD8+ T cells across distinct treatment groups, including control, anti–
PD-1 monotherapy, CEACAM1–TIM-3 blockade, and combination therapy.
First, combination therapy markedly reduced the proportion of Ceacam1+
neutrophils compared to all other groups (Response Fig. 6). In contrast, for Pd1-Tim3+
CD8+ T cells, the combination therapy increased their proportion compared to the
control group (Response Fig. 6).
Second, the proportion of Pd1+Tim3+ CD8+ T cells was elevated in all treatment
groups relative to the control group (Response Fig. 6). This finding suggests that
while combination therapy effectively targets myeloid-mediated immunosuppression,
it may not fully reverse or prevent the accumulation of highly exhausted CD8+ T cells
co-expressing both checkpoints. This incomplete reversal could be attributed to
persistent antigen exposure or compensatory feedback mechanisms within the tumor
microenvironment. Notably, compared with anti-PD-1 monotherapy, combination
therapy further downregulated the expression of multiple inhibitory immune
checkpoints including Pdcd1, Lag3, Havcr2, and Ctla4 on CD8+ T cells, indicating a
partial reversal of T cell exhaustion (Fig. 6h).
These findings highlight the dual-layered nature of the tumor immune response,
whereby effective modulation of the myeloid compartment does not automatically
translate into complete restoration of T cell functionality. We have now integrated
these results into Response Fig. 6 and expanded the accompanying text to discuss this
nuanced interplay (Lines 354-369). We believe this addition enriches the integrative
mechanistic framework of our study rather than simplifying it, by illustrating the
distinct dynamics of myeloid and lymphoid compartments under therapeutic pressure.
